Trade: Simulation dimensionality
Option: 2D planar, 3-DOF (r, theta, mass) as in MCR App. D
Pros: Reproduces the mission-analysis optimum exactly; episodes are short; reward shaping and the RL loop can be debugged in minutes
Cons: Cannot represent attitude, so it cannot answer either primary engineering question (thruster placement, sensor placement); no tip-over, no FOV occlusion, no yaw
Rationale / criteria: Used in Phase 1 to validate the RL plumbing against a known optimum, then retired
Revisit trigger: Never - it is a scaffold, not a deliverable

Trade: Simulation dimensionality
Option: 3D, 6-DOF rigid body with quaternion attitude
Pros: The only option that can answer thruster placement, torque authority, sensor boresight/FOV, lateral CoM trim and tip-over; matches the real GNC problem
Cons: Roughly 3x the state dimension, needs attitude control and thruster allocation, longer to get a first landing
Rationale / criteria: The project exists to answer 3D placement questions. Ilya is right that the marginal complexity is modest: the dynamics are a free rigid body, and the extra work is the thruster allocation layer, which is itself a deliverable

Trade: Physics / env backend
Option: Custom batched 6-DOF rigid-body integrator in PyTorch on CUDA
Pros: Variable mass (835 -> 500 kg, a 40% change) is trivial; every term is ours, so every assumption gets a params.csv row; thousands of parallel envs on one GPU; no contact engine overhead for a vehicle that is in free flight until the last 10 ms; stays in PyTorch, which Ilya already knows, and on-GPU with the policy
Cons: We write and verify the EOM ourselves; no contact model, so touchdown needs MuJoCo (see below)
Rationale / criteria: Decisive factor: the vehicle has no contacts during 99.9% of the episode, so a contact-physics engine buys nothing and costs mass-depletion awkwardness. Writing the EOM is also the aerospace norm (POST2, DSENDS)
Revisit trigger: If multi-body effects (propellant slosh, deploying legs) become important

Trade: Physics / env backend
Option: MuJoCo + MJX (JAX, GPU)
Decision: Selected for the touchdown / landing-gear study only
Pros: Best-in-class contact; honeycomb leg crush and slope tip-over come almost free; excellent offscreen renderer we want anyway
Cons: Mass depletion requires rebuilding batched model fields each step; JAX adds a second framework; overkill for free flight
Rationale / criteria: Used as a separate low-env-count study for phases below 1 m altitude, and as the renderer for the video

Trade: Physics / env backend
Option: NVIDIA Isaac Lab (the ETH RSL stack)
Pros: Literally the ETH RSL workflow; huge parallelism; mature domain randomisation
Cons: 2080 Super is Turing with 8 GB - at or below the Isaac Sim floor, and the install on WSL2 is fragile; its strength is contact-rich locomotion, which this problem does not have; heavy abstraction to learn on top of RL and GNC
Rationale / criteria: Rejected on hardware and on fit, NOT on method. The RSL method (thousands of parallel envs, domain randomisation, PPO via rsl_rl) is adopted in full - see TR-SIM-03
Revisit trigger: A GPU upgrade (>=16 GB Ampere+) plus a need for contact-rich or multi-robot scenes

Trade: Physics / env backend
Option: Basilisk (NASA/ASU astrodynamics framework)
Pros: Flight-grade spacecraft dynamics, proper actuator and sensor models, used in real missions
Cons: C++/SWIG, built for orbit and attitude rather than terminal landing; no GPU parallelism, so RL throughput is hopeless
Rationale / criteria: Worth reading for its sensor and actuator model structure; not worth adopting as the backend
Revisit trigger: If the project ever needs flight-qualifiable dynamics

Trade: RL algorithm library
Option: rsl_rl (ETH Robotic Systems Lab PPO)
Pros: It IS the RSL way, which is an explicit learning goal; PyTorch; expects exactly the batched-tensor VecEnv contract our env exposes; tiny and readable, so it can actually be studied
Cons: Thin documentation; fewer algorithms than SB3; assumes you supply the parallel env
Rationale / criteria: Gives the ETH RSL workflow without Isaac Sim. Reading its ~2k lines of PPO is itself a good chunk of goal 2

Trade: RL algorithm library
Option: Stable-Baselines3 (PPO / SAC)
Decision: SELECTED as the debug and cross-check path
Pros: Excellent docs; trustworthy reference implementations; works on a single gymnasium.Env, which is the right thing for the 3-DOF scaffold and for sanity-checking rsl_rl results
Cons: Single-env stepping is far too slow for the 6-DOF campaign
Rationale / criteria: Kept deliberately: if rsl_rl and SB3 disagree on the same env, the bug is in our env

Trade: RL algorithm library
Option: skrl
Pros: Supports both torch and JAX; clean multi-env API
Cons: Another abstraction layer to learn with no decisive advantage here
Rationale / criteria: No reason to prefer it over rsl_rl given the RSL learning goal

Trade: RL algorithm library
Option: PureJaxRL / rejax (end-to-end JAX PPO)
Pros: Fastest wall-clock by a wide margin; whole training loop JIT-compiled
Cons: Requires the env in JAX too, abandoning the PyTorch familiarity that makes this learnable
Rationale / criteria: Revisit only if PyTorch env throughput becomes the bottleneck
Revisit trigger: If a training run needs more than the 12 h overnight budget

Trade: Control architecture
Option: End-to-end RL: policy commands 4 throttles + 8 RCS valves directly
Pros: Maximum freedom; can exploit actuator coupling a human would not; one single learned artefact
Cons: Must learn attitude stabilisation from scratch before it can learn to land; 12 outputs, 8 of them discrete; needs ~100 Hz decisions, so episodes become 20k steps; near-impossible to debug or certify
Rationale / criteria: Not rejected forever - it is the interesting Phase 6 experiment, and worth comparing against the baseline once that exists
Revisit trigger: After the hierarchical policy lands reliably

Trade: Control architecture
Option: Hierarchical: RL guidance at 10 Hz commanding thrust magnitude + attitude, classical quaternion-feedback attitude controller at 100 Hz with a thruster-allocation layer
Pros: Episodes drop to a few thousand steps; the inner loop is deterministic, documentable and verifiable; the allocation layer is exactly the tool needed to study thruster placement; mirrors both the aerospace norm and the RSL pattern (RL sets targets, a fast low-level controller tracks them)
Cons: Caps achievable performance at whatever the inner loop can track; adds an interface to get right
Rationale / criteria: Standard in the RL-landing literature (Gaudet/Furfaro 6-DOF planetary landing) and in robotics RL. Also the only variant where thruster placement is a studiable parameter rather than something the network silently absorbs

Trade: Visualisation and telemetry
Option: Rerun (rerun-sdk)
Pros: Purpose-built for exactly this deliverable: synchronised 3D scene, time-series telemetry panels and camera images on one timeline, scrubbable; current de-facto standard for robotics telemetry; logging is a few lines per signal; .rrd recordings replay later
Cons: Young project with a moving API; not a photorealistic renderer
Rationale / criteria: Directly produces the 'telemetry + vehicle + policy' video the project is for, and is useful from day one for debugging

Trade: Visualisation and telemetry
Option: MuJoCo offscreen renderer -> mp4 via imageio-ffmpeg
Decision: SELECTED for the physical scene and the synthetic camera views
Pros: Physically consistent with the contact model; gives RGB and depth, so it doubles as the camera and lidar sensor renderer for validation frames
Cons: Plain-looking out of the box; needs lighting work to look good
Rationale / criteria: Pairs with Rerun: MuJoCo renders what the vehicle and its cameras see, Rerun composes the telemetry

Trade: Visualisation and telemetry
Option: Blender (import trajectory, render with Cycles/Eevee)
Decision: Deferred to the final video only
Pros: By far the best-looking result; proper regolith shading, plume glow, long shadows
Cons: Hours of work per shot; no feedback loop value
Rationale / criteria: Only worth it for the hero shot at the end, if at all
Revisit trigger: When the policy is final and the video is being cut

Trade: Visualisation and telemetry
Option: OpenCV for the animation
Pros: Already installed everywhere; fine for 2D drawing
Cons: Not a 3D renderer; no scene graph, no camera model, no timeline - reimplementing a viewer in it is wasted effort
Rationale / criteria: Keep OpenCV only for frame compositing and video encoding if ffmpeg is not enough. Answering Ilya's question directly: OpenCV is not the industry standard for this; Rerun and Foxglove are

Trade: Visualisation and telemetry
Option: Matplotlib
Pros: Right tool for Monte Carlo scatter, landing-ellipse CEP, dispersion histograms and the report figures
Cons: Not for animation
Rationale / criteria: Complementary, not competing

Trade: Episode span
Option: Full braking burn from 39 km to touchdown in one episode
Pros: Matches the real ConOps phase 7+8; no artificial handover
Cons: At 10 Hz guidance that is ~2100 steps with a 1400 m/s velocity change; credit assignment over that horizon from a sparse touchdown reward is the hardest possible first problem
Rationale / criteria: This is the Phase 5 target, reached by curriculum, not the Phase 3 starting point

Trade: Episode span
Option: Staged curriculum: terminal descent from 50 m, then powered descent from 2 km, then from 8 km (altimeter acquisition), then the full 39 km
Pros: Each stage has a dense, learnable signal; each stage initialises the next; the 8 km gate coincides with the real altimeter acquisition boundary, so the stages are physically meaningful, not arbitrary
Cons: Several training runs instead of one; needs a state-sampler per stage
Rationale / criteria: The 6-8 km altimeter acquisition altitude and the 50 m safety descent point are real ConOps boundaries (SIM-A12, SIM-A14), which makes the curriculum fall out of the mission design

Trade: Navigation in the loop
Option: Policy observes ground-truth state
Pros: Isolates the guidance problem; fast to train; gives the performance ceiling
Cons: Answers none of the sensor questions, which are a primary goal
Rationale / criteria: A necessary intermediate, explicitly not a result

Trade: Navigation in the loop
Option: Explicit EKF/MEKF fusing simulated IMU, star tracker, TRN fixes and altimeters; policy observes the filter estimate and its covariance
Pros: Mirrors the real avionics architecture in MCR 5.3; lets sensor dropouts and the no-altimeter gap above 6-8 km be studied directly; the covariance is a legitimate and informative policy input; separates navigation errors from control errors in the results
Cons: An EKF to implement and tune; its tuning becomes a confound
Rationale / criteria: This is the configuration that answers the sensor-placement and noise questions, which is the point of the project

Trade: Navigation in the loop
Option: End-to-end: policy observes raw sensor streams, with recurrence, and learns its own state estimate
Pros: Potentially better than a hand-tuned EKF; a genuinely interesting research result; strong literature precedent
Cons: Needs recurrent policies and far more samples; very hard to attribute failures
Rationale / criteria: Good final experiment and a strong learning exercise, once the EKF baseline exists to compare against
Revisit trigger: After the EKF configuration meets the accuracy requirement

Trade: Attitude actuation architecture
Option: Differential throttle on 4 fixed main engines + 8 canted cold-gas RCS in 4 pods on the upper deck
Pros: Matches the brief (4 side-mounted mains, cold gas on top, Blue Ghost style); differential throttle gives strong pitch/roll authority (0.21 kNm at 150 N differential = 1.6 rad/s2); RCS supplies the yaw authority the mains cannot
Cons: 4 parallel vertical engines produce only Fz, Mx, My - rank 3, so yaw depends entirely on RCS; RCS cross-coupling needs an allocation solver
Rationale / criteria: See the actuation-rank note in PLAN.md: 4 parallel mains cannot produce yaw torque at all, so some RCS is not optional
Revisit trigger: If the propulsion team fixes the engine count or adds gimbals

Trade: Attitude actuation architecture
Option: 12 RCS thrusters arranged as 6 pure couples
Pros: Clean decoupled 3-axis control; textbook allocation; single-fault tolerant with 16
Cons: 50% more thrusters, plumbing and dry mass for authority the differential throttle already provides in pitch and roll
Rationale / criteria: Model it as a sim option so the placement study can quantify what the extra 4 thrusters buy
Revisit trigger: If the 8-thruster layout cannot hold attitude during a main-engine-out case

Trade: Attitude actuation architecture
Option: Gimballed main engines (TVC)
Pros: Large control authority with no extra propellant path; standard for single-engine landers
Cons: Actuators, flexible feed lines and mass; redundant when you already have 4 independently throttled engines
Rationale / criteria: Differential throttle is the natural TVC equivalent for a 4-engine cluster
Revisit trigger: If the engine count drops to 1 or 2

Trade: How to hover at touchdown mass (13.5% of Tmax needed, engines floor near 30%)
Option: Specify deep-throttle main engines (floor near 10%)
Pros: Simplest control architecture; all 4 engines stay symmetric to touchdown
Cons: Deep throttling a pressure-fed bipropellant engine costs combustion stability margin and Isp; may not exist off the shelf in the LEROS 4 class
Rationale / criteria: Flagged to Mattia (PRP). P-13 minimum throttle is TBD, so the sim treats 30% as an LLM assumption (SIM-P04) and sweeps it UPDATE 31.10.2026: Mattia gives 3-6 kN. At <=5 kN two-engine terminal hover works and the contradiction largely dissolves; 6 kN was the bad corner. The trade becomes hoverability vs the propellant cost of a longer burn (SIM-P18).
Revisit trigger: When P-13 gets a real value

Trade: How to hover at touchdown mass (13.5% of Tmax needed, engines floor near 30%)
Option: Shut down 2 of 4 engines for terminal descent
Pros: No new hardware; 2 engines at 30% give 900 N against 812 N of weight, so hovering becomes possible
Cons: Only 11% thrust margin; shutdown transient at low altitude; the surviving pair must be diametrically opposite or the vehicle gets a large pitch bias; loses one differential-throttle axis exactly when it is needed most
Rationale / criteria: Cheap to model and a clean sim experiment. The lost torque axis makes RCS authority critical UPDATE 31.10.2026: Mattia gives 3-6 kN. At <=5 kN two-engine terminal hover works and the contradiction largely dissolves; 6 kN was the bad corner. The trade becomes hoverability vs the propellant cost of a longer burn (SIM-P18).
Revisit trigger: Compare against option A and C once P-13 is known

Trade: How to hover at touchdown mass (13.5% of Tmax needed, engines floor near 30%)
Option: Bipropellant RCS thrusters take over terminal descent, mains off below the safety descent point
Pros: Already the MCR 5.2.3 baseline ('RCS thrusters will be employed to assist the descent burn and provide the fine throttleability required for terminal touchdown'); fine control authority; no deep-throttle requirement on the mains
Cons: Needs ~812 N from the RCS tier, far above a cold-gas system, so this is a third propulsion tier; main-engine shutdown at 50 m is a committed, irreversible event
Rationale / criteria: Most likely the real answer, and it reframes the sim: terminal descent is a different actuator set, not a throttled-down version of the braking burn UPDATE 31.10.2026: Mattia gives 3-6 kN. At <=5 kN two-engine terminal hover works and the contradiction largely dissolves; 6 kN was the bad corner. The trade becomes hoverability vs the propellant cost of a longer burn (SIM-P18).
Revisit trigger: Confirm the RCS thrust class with Mattia

Trade: Ground-relative velocity sensing
Option: Config 1: vision feature tracking + laser and radar altimeters (MCR baseline)
Pros: 2.14 kg, 27.2 W; vision-only TRN has flown (Blue Ghost M1 touched down 58 m from the targeted ellipse); laser + radar + vision dissimilarity
Cons: Horizontal velocity is indirect, and its accuracy is TBD - the single biggest unquantified risk to meeting the touchdown limits
Rationale / criteria: MCR 5.3.8 states the choice is open pending touchdown limits (IF-11). Producing the number that closes it is a headline deliverable of this project DECIDED: Ilya selected Config 1 as the starting point 31.10.2026. The sim still reports what Config 2 would buy, but Config 1 is the baseline to model.

Trade: Ground-relative velocity sensing
Option: Config 2: add Doppler LIDAR (LUNA) for direct 3-axis velocity
Decision: Deferred - sim reports the delta only
Pros: Direct 3-axis velocity measurement; removes the dominant terminal-descent uncertainty
Cons: +3.02 kg and about +5.6 kg of propellant; not flown until IM-4 in 2027; power not published
Rationale / criteria: The sim should report the landing-accuracy and touchdown-violation rate for both configs; that comparison is the engineering output that justifies 3 kg

Trade: Classical guidance baseline to benchmark the policy against
Option: Convex powered-descent guidance (lossless convexification, Acikmese & Ploen) solved with cvxpy
Pros: Globally optimal for the relaxed problem and provably equivalent to the original; the recognised standard for propulsive landing; gives a hard optimality bound the policy can be measured against; handles the thrust lower bound, which is the crux of TR-SIM-09
Cons: Needs a solver in the loop; 3-DOF unless extended; assumes a known state, so it is not robust to navigation error by itself
Rationale / criteria: Having a verified optimal baseline is what makes an RL result credible to an aerospace reviewer, and it also cross-validates the dynamics against MCR App. D

Trade: Classical guidance baseline to benchmark the policy against
Option: ZEM/ZEV (zero-effort-miss / zero-effort-velocity) feedback guidance
Pros: Closed-form, trivial to implement, runs at any rate, and is the natural thing to put inside the Monte Carlo as the robust-but-suboptimal reference
Cons: Not fuel-optimal; ignores thrust bounds; needs a time-to-go estimate
Rationale / criteria: Cheap to add and it is the honest comparison point - what a conventional lander would actually fly

Trade: Classical guidance baseline to benchmark the policy against
Option: Apollo polynomial guidance
Pros: Flight-proven; historically interesting
Cons: Tuned for the LM; strictly dominated by the two options above as a benchmark
Rationale / criteria: Read about it, do not implement it

Trade: Landing-surface representation
Option: Flat plane with a slope
Pros: Trivial; analytic altitude; fast
Cons: No hazards, no roughness, so altimeter and stereo models are meaningless
Rationale / criteria: Fine while the guidance problem is being solved

Trade: Landing-surface representation
Option: Procedurally randomised heightmap: slope + fractal roughness + craters and rocks
Pros: Supports the randomised-surface Monte Carlo the brief asks for; cheap raycasting for altimeters and lidar on GPU; hazard density becomes a parameter (SIM-E08); generated per env, so it costs nothing at scale
Cons: Not a real lunar surface, so TRN crater matching against it is synthetic
Rationale / criteria: The right fidelity for GNC robustness work; the parameters are what matters, not photographic realism

Trade: Landing-surface representation
Option: Real LRO NAC / LOLA DEM of the target region
Pros: Real terrain statistics; makes TRN crater matching genuine; MCR 5.3.5 already cites LRO NAC at 0.5 m/px for launch-site refinement
Cons: Large downloads and preprocessing; one fixed site, so it cannot be randomised; overkill before the pipeline works
Rationale / criteria: Worth it later for the video and for a realistic TRN demonstration
Revisit trigger: When TRN is modelled from rendered images rather than as a synthetic position fix

Trade: Where hazard detection and avoidance (HDA) happens
Option: Keep HDA in terminal descent from the 50 m safety descent point, as ConOps phase 8 states
Pros: No change to the ConOps; shortest exposure; hazard is seen at the highest possible resolution
Cons: Divert capability from 50 m with 6 s to go is 5.3 m at 20 deg tilt (SIM-H05), against the ~30 m needed (SIM-H02). The 3.5 s perception latency (SIM-H07) alone consumes most of the 6 s. Stereo from 50 m sees only a few tens of metres of ground.
Rationale / criteria: Quantitatively infeasible, by roughly a factor of six in divert distance and with no time budget left. This is a ConOps problem, not a controller tuning problem.

Trade: Where hazard detection and avoidance (HDA) happens
Option: Move HDA up into the lower braking burn: detect and commit at 300-500 m, divert before the safety descent point
Pros: Divert capability becomes 35-150 m at 10-20 deg tilt (SIM-H06) - comfortably above SIM-H02; stereo and the wide-FOV camera still resolve 0.3 m hazards at that range; the 50 m point then becomes a clean, already-safe vertical descent, which is what the ConOps actually assumes
Cons: Changes ConOps phase 7/8; the vehicle is still pitched over at 300-500 m, so the hazard camera may not see the landing site (interacts with TR-SIM-14); needs propellant margin reserved for the divert
Rationale / criteria: The only option where the geometry and the timeline both close. Also matches how ALHAT/SPLICE-class systems are designed - detection happens hundreds of metres up.
Revisit trigger: If a scanning lidar is added, which would extend detection range

Trade: Where hazard detection and avoidance (HDA) happens
Option: No onboard HDA: pre-select the site from LRO NAC orbital imagery and land blind
Pros: LRO NAC is 0.5 m/px, already cited in MCR 5.3.5; removes the hardest perception problem entirely; no divert propellant needed
Cons: Only works if landing accuracy is good enough that the pre-cleared ellipse is guaranteed hazard-free - i.e. it converts a perception requirement into a 50 m landing-accuracy requirement (SIM-T01); no protection against anything below LRO resolution
Rationale / criteria: Genuinely viable and should be costed, because it is the cheapest answer. The sim can decide it: if the MC landing radius is well inside a verified-clear ellipse, onboard HDA may be unnecessary.
Revisit trigger: After the Phase 5 Monte Carlo gives a landing-radius distribution

Trade: Sensor pointing given that the vehicle flies pitched ~68 deg from vertical during the braking burn
Option: Body-fixed boresights along -Z (the implicit MCR assumption)
Pros: Simplest; no mechanisms; no pointing budget
Cons: At 68 deg tilt a 'nadir' camera looks 22 deg below the HORIZON (SIM-A17), and a nadir altimeter sees a slant range 2.7x the altitude, so DLEM 30 acquires at 2.6 km rather than 6-8 km (SIM-A18). Both primary descent sensors are mispointed for most of the burn.
Rationale / criteria: MCR 5.3.5 already flags the camera half of this as TBC. The altimeter half appears not to have been noticed, and it widens the altimeter-free stretch from 39->8 km to 39->2.6 km.

Trade: Sensor pointing given that the vehicle flies pitched ~68 deg from vertical during the braking burn
Option: Cant the descent sensors ~60-68 deg from body -Z so they point at nadir during the burn
Decision: SELECTED as the sim baseline to evaluate
Pros: No moving parts; points correctly exactly when TRN and altimetry matter most; a fixed cant is cheap to analyse and to test
Cons: Mispointed during the vertical phases, when the vehicle is upright - so terminal descent then needs its own sensor set; cant angle is only optimal for one trajectory
Rationale / criteria: The natural fix and cheap to study: cant angle becomes a swept parameter and the sim reports navigation error vs cant. This is the one genuine sensor-PLACEMENT question the sim answers well.

Trade: Sensor pointing given that the vehicle flies pitched ~68 deg from vertical during the braking burn
Option: Two sensor sets: canted for the burn, nadir for the vertical phases
Pros: Each phase is correctly instrumented; the MCR already has two cameras with different FOVs and three altimeters of two types, so the hardware may already support this with the right mounting
Cons: More units or more mounting complexity; more interfaces
Rationale / criteria: Probably where this lands, since MCR Table 10 already switches sensors by phase. The sim should confirm which units need which pointing.

Trade: Sensor pointing given that the vehicle flies pitched ~68 deg from vertical during the braking burn
Option: Gimballed or steered sensor platform
Pros: Always correctly pointed; one set of units
Cons: Mechanism mass, power, a pointing-knowledge error budget, and a new single-point failure - against a low-cost COTS design philosophy (AVI-11)
Rationale / criteria: Disproportionate for a 3.57 kg subsystem

Trade: Guidance method that the engineering results are based on
Option: Classical: convex powered-descent guidance plus ZEM/ZEV, as in TR-SIM-11
Pros: This is actual flight practice for propulsive landing; verifiable and provably optimal for the relaxed problem; credible to an MCR/PDR reviewer; deterministic, so sensitivity sweeps are clean
Cons: Does not by itself handle non-convex hazard avoidance or navigation-error robustness
Rationale / criteria: IMPORTANT EXPECTATION SETTING: no flown spacecraft uses RL for powered descent. The numbers that go to the subsystem teams must come from the classical baseline, or the results will not be trusted.

Trade: Guidance method that the engineering results are based on
Option: Reinforcement learning guidance
Decision: SELECTED for the learning goal and as a research comparison
Pros: Handles what convex optimisation struggles with: non-convex hazard avoidance with a discrete site choice, direct robustness to navigation error, and actuator constraints the convex form cannot express; active research area (Gaudet/Furfaro 6-DOF planetary landing); it is goal 2 of the project
Cons: No flight heritage anywhere; not certifiable today; results are only as good as the reward shaping, which is easy to get subtly wrong
Rationale / criteria: Keep it, but position it honestly as a research comparison against the classical baseline rather than as a proposed flight algorithm

Trade: Total maximum thrust Tmax within Mattia's 3-6 kN range
Option: Bottom of range, ~3 kN
Pros: 4-engine hover throttle is 27.1%, within 3 points of a 30% floor, so a modest deep-throttle spec buys full symmetric terminal descent; 2-engine hover trivial at 54%; gentler structural loads; smaller nozzles ease the 0.6 m ground-clearance problem (SIM-G13)
Cons: Braking burn roughly doubles to ~430 s, costing an estimated 30-60 kg more propellant (SIM-P18); lower T/W margin for abort or divert
Rationale / criteria: Best for controllability, worst for propellant. Phase 1 quantifies the exchange rate.
Revisit trigger: After the Phase 1 Tmax sweep

Trade: Total maximum thrust Tmax within Mattia's 3-6 kN range
Option: Top of range, 6 kN (the MCR placeholder)
Pros: Shortest burn, least gravity loss, lowest propellant; matches the existing MCR trajectory solution so no re-optimisation needed
Cons: Uniquely bad for terminal descent: neither 4-engine nor 2-engine hover is possible at a 30% floor (SIM-P17), forcing a deep-throttle spec or a separate bipropellant RCS tier
Rationale / criteria: The one value in the range that creates the hover problem. Worth knowing that the MCR's placeholder happened to land on the worst corner.

Trade: Total maximum thrust Tmax within Mattia's 3-6 kN range
Option: Middle, 4-5 kN
Pros: 2-engine terminal hover works (SIM-P17 limit is 5.4 kN); propellant penalty is small (est. 0-30 kg vs 6 kN); keeps reasonable T/W margin
Cons: Terminal descent is asymmetric on two engines, losing one differential-throttle axis and raising the demand on RCS yaw/roll authority
Rationale / criteria: Probably where this lands. The sim should report landing accuracy and propellant for 3/4/5/6 kN and let propulsion choose.

Trade: Scope of the thruster-placement question (Ilya notes the payload and layout are modular, so placement is genuinely free)
Option: Treat placement as fixed; sim answers sizing only
Decision: SUPERSEDED - my earlier position was too narrow
Pros: Keeps the sim simple
Cons: Wastes the design freedom that actually exists; the dynamics-relevant geometry IS free on this vehicle
Rationale / criteria: Withdrawn. Ilya is right: with a modular deck layout, the torque arms and cant angles are design variables, not givens.

Trade: Scope of the thruster-placement question (Ilya notes the payload and layout are modular, so placement is genuinely free)
Option: Make the dynamics-relevant geometry first-class swept parameters: main-engine radius and cant, RCS pod radius and cant, sensor boresight cant
Pros: Everything that enters the control-effectiveness matrix becomes a sweep: main-engine radial offset (SIM-G08), engine cant, RCS pod radius and cant (SIM-G15/G16), sensor cant (TR-SIM-14). Builds the B matrix from the geometry rows so moving a thruster is a CSV edit, not a code change
Cons: Does not cover the constraints that live outside the dynamics
Rationale / criteria: The right scope. The sim optimises geometry against control authority, propellant and landing accuracy.

Trade: Scope of the thruster-placement question (Ilya notes the payload and layout are modular, so placement is genuinely free)
Option: Also derive the allowable payload CoM envelope from trim authority
Pros: Modularity cuts both ways: if payloads mount on either face of either deck (S1.2.1), the CoM moves laterally and vertically between configurations, changing trim demand, torque arms and tip-over margin. The sim can invert this into an allowable CoM box for the Payload ICD (SIM-M11)
Cons: Needs a trim-authority criterion agreed with propulsion
Rationale / criteria: This is the placement question modularity actually creates, and it produces a number the Payload ICD currently lacks. Constraints outside the dynamics - plume impingement on a lower-deck payload, FOV blockage, harness routing, thermal - stay with CAD and STR.

Trade: Braking-burn ignition altitude (MCR says 39 km; simulation says that is infeasible)
Option: Keep 39 km and raise the thrust to ~9.4 kN
Pros: Preserves the MCR's stated ConOps number; shortest burn (140 s) and least propellant (~330 kg)
Cons: 9.36 kN is 1.56x the top of Mattia's 3-6 kN range (SIM-A20); would mean 2.34 kN per engine and makes the terminal hover problem far worse (TR-SIM-09)
Rationale / criteria: Not available with the current propulsion concept. Worth stating to Freddy as the thrust that 39 km would actually demand.
Revisit trigger: If the engine selection moves above 8 kN total

Trade: Braking-burn ignition altitude (MCR says 39 km; simulation says that is infeasible)
Option: Raise ignition to ~60 km at 6 kN (altitude scales with 1/thrust: 138/96/75/62 km for 3/4/5/6 kN)
Pros: Feasible across the whole 3-6 kN range; the reference guidance lands inside the touchdown box from 60 km using 380 kg; burn 221 s, close to the MCR's own 202 s figure
Cons: Costs propellant (380 kg vs the 335 kg previously assumed); lengthens the TRN-only navigation stretch, since altimeters still only acquire at ~2.6 km when pitched over (SIM-A18)
Rationale / criteria: Two of the MCR's own numbers already point here: the 202 s burn duration implies ~55 km, and 6 kN implies ~62 km. Only the 39 km figure in sec. 5.3.5 disagrees, and it is marked TBC.
Revisit trigger: When Freddy re-runs the multiphase optimisation

Trade: Braking-burn ignition altitude (MCR says 39 km; simulation says that is infeasible)
Option: Arrive on a shallower arc (depressed trajectory) so the descent rate at ignition is lower
Pros: Attacks the root cause: the problem is the 557 m/s descent rate on arrival, not the altitude as such. A lofted or depressed arc trades hop delta-v for a gentler approach
Cons: Any departure from the minimum-energy arc costs ascent delta-v, and the hop is already delta-v critical (P-09)
Rationale / criteria: The genuinely interesting option and nobody has costed it. Needs the ascent and braking burns optimised together, which is Freddy's multiphase problem, not this simulation's.
Revisit trigger: Raise at the next mission-analysis review

Trade: Main-engine throttle cap: differential throttle needs headroom to produce torque
Option: Command up to 100% of Tmax
Pros: Maximum braking performance; lowest propellant; matches how the 3-DOF model and MCR App. D treat thrust
Cons: At 100% there is zero throttle headroom, so differential-throttle torque is zero and attitude authority collapses from 8.45 to the RCS-only 0.234 rad/s2. Measured: 131 Nm delivered against a 460 Nm demand, vehicle tumbles past 175 deg.
Rationale / criteria: A 3-DOF model cannot show this, because thrust direction is an instantaneous control there. It is the first genuinely new result from going to 6-DOF.

Trade: Main-engine throttle cap: differential throttle needs headroom to produce torque
Option: Cap main throttle at ~90%, reserving headroom for attitude control
Decision: SELECTED, but not yet sufficient on its own
Pros: Restores ~2 rad/s2 of pitch/roll authority; simple; no new hardware
Cons: Cuts usable thrust by 10%, which lengthens the braking burn and raises the required ignition altitude (SIM-A19/A21) - so it feeds straight back into the TR-SIM-16 thrust trade. And 2 rad/s2 is still below what the current attitude gains demand.
Rationale / criteria: Right direction, insufficient alone. The attitude bandwidth must come down to match the authority, or the authority must go up (bigger RCS, canted mains, gimbals).
Revisit trigger: After the omega_n sweep completes

Trade: Main-engine throttle cap: differential throttle needs headroom to produce torque
Option: Raise RCS thrust so attitude authority does not depend on main-engine throttle state
Pros: Decouples attitude control from the braking throttle entirely, which is the clean architectural answer; also fixes the 36x yaw weakness
Cons: 22 N cold-gas thrusters (SIM-P09) give only 0.234 rad/s2; reaching ~2 rad/s2 independently would need roughly an order of magnitude more thrust, i.e. a bipropellant RCS tier - which is what MCR 5.2.3 already implies and what TR-SIM-09 option C proposes for terminal descent
Rationale / criteria: Note the convergence: the deep-throttle problem and the attitude-authority problem may have the same answer, a bipropellant RCS tier. Worth raising with Mattia as one question, not two.
Revisit trigger: Phase 2 completion

Trade: Closing the landing-accuracy requirement (SIM-T01, 50 m)
Option: Velocity-only profile guidance plus open-loop alignment of the ignition point
Pros: Meets the requirement: 21 m miss with 0.98 m/s vertical, 0.00 m/s horizontal, upright. Soft, fuel-efficient (427 kg), and the alignment converges in 4 passes.
Cons: Purely open loop in position - no feedback at all. A dispersion at ignition propagates straight through to the landing point, so this says nothing about robustness.
Rationale / criteria: Correct answer for a nominal reference trajectory and for the Phase 1/2 acceptance gates. It is the baseline, not the flight design.
Revisit trigger: Phase 5 Monte Carlo

Trade: Closing the landing-accuracy requirement (SIM-T01, 50 m)
Option: ZEM/ZEV position feedback
Pros: Standard closed-loop soft-landing law; improved the miss 3.5x (2374 -> 685 m) on its first try
Cons: Demands ~27 m/s2 at ignition against ~5.7 available, so it saturates hard, burns the tanks dry at 450 kg and arrives at 21.7 m/s vertical and 107 m/s horizontal
Rationale / criteria: The failure is informative: this vehicle is thrust-limited enough that aggressive position feedback is not affordable early in the burn. A feasible version needs a proper optimal t_go and must stay inside the thrust bound - i.e. the convex formulation (TR-SIM-11), not naive ZEM/ZEV.
Revisit trigger: Phase 3

Trade: Closing the landing-accuracy requirement (SIM-T01, 50 m)
Option: Range-to-go velocity profile, v_des = sqrt(2 a_brake d) toward the site
Pros: Self-limiting by construction and symmetric with the vertical law; no gain tuning against a thrust bound
Cons: Keeps speed high until close and then cannot brake in time: arrives 1335 m out at 190 m/s horizontal. The vertical profile already fixes the time to ground, so the horizontal channel cannot independently satisfy both the range and the velocity constraint
Rationale / criteria: Shows the real structure of the problem: with the descent timeline fixed by the vertical profile, horizontal range and horizontal velocity are not independently controllable. Either the vertical timeline must be part of the optimisation (convex/RL), or the ignition point must be chosen to make them consistent - which is what the open-loop alignment does.
Revisit trigger: Phase 3

Trade: How to train the landing policy: from scratch, cloned, or cloned then fine-tuned
Option: PPO from scratch
Pros: No expert needed, so no classical law has to exist first; the policy is free to find solutions the classical law cannot express
Cons: Four runs, 9.7e9 environment steps, best result 0.1% soft landings and 38 m/s mean impact. The vehicle plateaus at a controlled-crash policy: it learns to point retrograde and throttle, but never the terminal flare
Rationale / criteria: The reward is dense and the dynamics are correct, so this is an exploration failure, not a reward failure: a successful touchdown is a measure-zero event at random initialisation, and nothing in 1e10 samples stumbles onto it often enough to reinforce. Exactly the regime behaviour cloning exists for.
Revisit trigger: If the curriculum is rebuilt to start the policy a few metres up and extend downward, from-scratch may become viable - worth one run.

Trade: How to train the landing policy: from scratch, cloned, or cloned then fine-tuned
Option: Behaviour cloning only
Pros: Converges in 300 iterations (~45 min); inherits the classical law's stability; no reward-hacking risk at all
Cons: Caps out at 31.7% soft / 109 m miss, strictly WORSE than the expert it clones, because an MLP trained on the mean action cannot reproduce the expert's switching behaviour near touchdown
Rationale / criteria: Useful as an initialiser, not as a product. Note the asymmetry: BC can only approach the expert's performance, so it can never answer the question the project is actually asking (can a learned policy beat classical guidance when rate limits and actuator lag are added?).
Revisit trigger: N/A - kept as the first stage of the selected option

Trade: How to train the landing policy: from scratch, cloned, or cloned then fine-tuned
Option: Behaviour cloning, then PPO fine-tuning (SELECTED)
Pros: 76.1% soft landings, 2.4x the BC baseline and ~700x the from-scratch result, in 25 PPO iterations (10 min). Mean impact 3.41 m/s vertical against 38 m/s from scratch. Holds at 73.1% by iteration 50
Cons: Requires a working classical expert first, so it cannot be the method for a problem where none exists. Fragile handoff: needs a critic warm-up and reduced exploration noise or it destroys the cloned policy outright (SIM-RL10, SIM-RL11). Still misses the 50 m accuracy requirement at 95 m
Rationale / criteria: This is the standard practice in robotics learning for exactly this reason, and the failure mode is worth recording: the first attempt collapsed from 43% to 0% soft because PPO started with an untrained critic and std=0.50. Both are handoff bugs, not algorithmic ones. The accuracy shortfall is the open item - the horizontal shaping weight (0.02/m) is an order below the altitude weight in effect, so the policy has little incentive to close the last 100 m laterally.
Revisit trigger: Raise the horizontal shaping weight and retrain; if the miss stays near 95 m the limit is the 10 Hz action rate, not the reward.

Trade: Config 1 (camera feature tracking) vs Config 2 (Doppler LIDAR, +3 kg) - resolved with numbers
Option: Config 1: camera feature tracking fused with IMU (MCR baseline)
Decision: Marginal - proceed only with a real SIM-S34
Pros: No mass or power cost; already in the baseline; gives the same POSITION knowledge as Config 2 (18.6 m vs 17.0 m mean at touchdown), so the landing-accuracy requirement SIM-T01 does not distinguish the two
Cons: Touchdown velocity knowledge is 0.23 m/s mean and 0.42 m/s at the 95th percentile against a 0.5 m/s requirement (SIM-T03). Navigation error alone eats 84% of the budget, leaving essentially nothing for control error. The vehicle cannot verify the requirement it is being held to
Rationale / criteria: The trade turns entirely on SIM-S34, the per-measurement camera velocity accuracy, which is an Assumption (LLM) of 0.5 m/s. If the real figure is better than ~0.3 m/s Config 1 is comfortable; if it is worse, Config 1 cannot meet SIM-T03 at all. This is the single highest-value number Nicola can provide.
Revisit trigger: Nicola's Config 1 velocity-accuracy estimate; re-run scripts/run_nav.py --seeds 20 with it

Trade: Config 1 (camera feature tracking) vs Config 2 (Doppler LIDAR, +3 kg) - resolved with numbers
Option: Config 2: Doppler LIDAR (LUNA), direct 3-axis velocity
Pros: Touchdown velocity knowledge 0.01 m/s - 2% of the SIM-T03 budget instead of 84%. Removes the dependency on SIM-S34 entirely, and with it the risk that the whole terminal-descent architecture has to change late. Works in the plume-dust regime where cameras do not
Cons: +3 kg, plus power and a data interface. Buys NOTHING for position knowledge (17.0 m vs 18.6 m), so it cannot be justified on landing accuracy - only on touchdown velocity
Rationale / criteria: Buying 3 kg of margin against the one requirement the baseline cannot comfortably verify looks like good value, but the honest statement is that the decision is not resolvable until SIM-S34 is real. What the simulation HAS settled is that the argument is about SIM-T03 and nothing else: position accuracy is not a discriminator.
Revisit trigger: Same as above; also revisit if the dry-mass budget tightens

Trade: Does the altitude-priority profile guidance law meet the landing-accuracy requirement under dispersion?
Option: Keep the profile law (velocity-profile tracking, open loop in position)
Pros: Lands the NOMINAL case at 21 m meeting all five touchdown criteria; simple, needs no onboard optimisation, no convergence risk, and runs comfortably at 10 Hz
Cons: Under nominal injection dispersions the CEP is 4447 m and R95 is 8326 m against a 50 m requirement: 0 of 24 cases pass. It also exhausted the tanks in 11 of 24 cases. The law controls VELOCITY profiles and never looks at where the landing site is, so an injection velocity error integrates unattenuated over a 222 s burn
Rationale / criteria: This is the decisive negative result of the project so far. It is not a tuning problem - the nominal lands at 21 m. Accuracy under the current law is set entirely by injection accuracy, and meeting 50 m would need injection velocity knowledge of roughly 0.2 m/s, which is not achievable. Closed-loop position guidance is therefore MANDATORY, not an optimisation.
Revisit trigger: N/A - superseded. Retain the law as the verification baseline and as the behaviour-cloning expert.

Trade: Does the altitude-priority profile guidance law meet the landing-accuracy requirement under dispersion?
Option: Convex powered-descent guidance (lossless convexification, TR-SIM-11)
Pros: Targets the landing SITE with the thrust bound respected by construction, which is exactly what both earlier position-feedback attempts failed at (TR-SIM-20: naive ZEM/ZEV demands 27 m/s2 against 5.7 available, and the range-to-go profile cannot satisfy range and velocity simultaneously because the vertical channel already fixes the timeline). Flight heritage on this problem class
Cons: Needs an onboard solver and a convergence guarantee, which is real avionics work, and the OBC budget has not been assessed. Not yet implemented here
Rationale / criteria: The two cheaper options have both been tried and both fail for the same structural reason: with the descent timeline fixed by a vertical profile, horizontal range and horizontal velocity are not independently controllable. The vertical timeline has to be part of the optimisation. That is what the convex formulation does and why it is the standard answer.
Revisit trigger: Implement and re-run scripts/mc_campaign.py; compare CEP directly

Trade: Does the altitude-priority profile guidance law meet the landing-accuracy requirement under dispersion?
Option: Relax the requirement to 100 m radius (the S1.1.3 / P-08 reading)
Pros: Would be free, and the requirement conflict is genuine and unresolved - GNC-01 says a 100 m diameter circle while S1.1.3 and P-08 say 100 m radius
Cons: Irrelevant at this error magnitude: the CEP is 4447 m, so a 2x looser requirement changes nothing. 0 of 24 cases would pass at 100 m either
Rationale / criteria: Worth recording explicitly so nobody proposes it later as a shortcut. The requirement conflict still needs resolving (Ilya owes this) but it is not on the critical path for the accuracy problem.
Revisit trigger: N/A

Trade: Which lever closes the landing-accuracy requirement: sensors, engine tolerance, injection accuracy, or the guidance law?
Option: Buy better sensors
Pros: Config 2 Doppler LIDAR exists and is characterised (TR-SIM-22); would be a procurement decision rather than new development
Cons: Landing miss shows NO usable trend with sensor noise: 39/239/119/310/88 m as the noise is scaled 0 to 5x with the handover error held fixed, and a 5x degraded suite landed closer than a near-perfect one (SIM-NV08). Navigation error itself scales cleanly (0.3 to 40 m, SIM-NV07), so the estimator is fine - the miss simply does not depend on it
Rationale / criteria: The guidance law has no position feedback, so it converts whatever navigation transient occurs into an uncorrected landing offset regardless of how small that transient is. Sensor quality cannot be the binding constraint while that is true. Revisit AFTER closed-loop guidance exists, where sensor noise should start to matter.
Revisit trigger: Re-run scripts/noise_study.py once convex guidance is implemented

Trade: Which lever closes the landing-accuracy requirement: sensors, engine tolerance, injection accuracy, or the guidance law?
Option: Tighten engine thrust tolerance
Pros: Engine dispersion IS the dominant error source - it alone gives a 3251 m CEP with injection dispersion switched off entirely, and it also causes the propellant exhaustion in 25-35% of cases
Cons: CEP scales linearly at ~1600 m per percent of thrust tolerance (SIM-MC19), so meeting 50 m needs 0.03% - two orders below the 1-3% a real pressure-fed bipropellant engine delivers
Rationale / criteria: Identifying the dominant error source correctly does not make it the right lever. This is the most useful negative result of the campaign: it closes off the obvious engineering response and forces the guidance change.
Revisit trigger: N/A - physically unachievable

Trade: Which lever closes the landing-accuracy requirement: sensors, engine tolerance, injection accuracy, or the guidance law?
Option: Tighten injection accuracy (TR-08)
Pros: Would be mission-analysis work rather than hardware; the dispersion is currently unknown (SIM-A15) so there was reason to think it mattered
Cons: Scaling the injection dispersion from zero to full moves the CEP by less than the 48-case sampling uncertainty: 3251 / 2492 / 2452 / 2438 / 3005 / 3574 m (SIM-MC17). The engine floor dominates completely
Rationale / criteria: Worth recording because this was my own first hypothesis and the data refuted it. TR-08 is still needed for other reasons, but not for landing accuracy.
Revisit trigger: N/A

Trade: Which lever closes the landing-accuracy requirement: sensors, engine tolerance, injection accuracy, or the guidance law?
Option: Replace the guidance law with closed-loop position guidance (convex, TR-SIM-11)
Pros: The only lever left once the other three are eliminated by measurement. Targets the landing SITE with the thrust bound respected by construction, and would make engine and injection dispersion correctable rather than integrated. Flight heritage on this problem class
Cons: Needs an onboard solver and a convergence guarantee; OBC budget unassessed; not yet implemented here, so the claim that it fixes the problem is an expectation rather than a measurement
Rationale / criteria: This is now a conclusion by elimination rather than a preference: sensors do not matter, engine tolerance is unachievable, injection accuracy does not matter. The remaining degree of freedom is the law itself. TR-SIM-20 additionally shows why the two cheap position-feedback laws fail, so it has to be the full formulation with the vertical timeline inside the optimisation.
Revisit trigger: Implement, then re-run mc_campaign.py and noise_study.py and compare CEP directly
